drug_name: Etonogestrel and Ethinyl Estradiol Vaginal Ring
what_its_for: This is a birth control (contraceptive) ring used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (etonogestrel) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (egg release), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and thin the lining of the uterus.
how_to_take: The ring is a small, flexible plastic ring that you insert into your vagina yourself. Squeeze the ring between your thumb and index finger and gently push it into your vagina as far as it will comfortably go. You do not need to place it in a specific position — just make sure it feels comfortable and is not causing discomfort. Leave the ring in place for 3 weeks (21 days), then remove it for 1 week (7 days). To remove, hook your finger under the rim and gently pull it out. After the 7-day ring-free week, insert a new ring. If the ring slips out accidentally, rinse it with cool or lukewarm water (never hot water) and reinsert it as soon as possible.
dosing: Insert one vaginal ring and wear it continuously for 21 days (3 weeks). Remove the ring on the same day of the week it was inserted, at approximately the same time of day. Keep it out for 7 days (1 ring-free week), then insert a new ring. Your period will typically occur during the ring-free week. Start the first ring on the first day of your menstrual period, or as directed by your doctor. If you start on a day other than day 1 of your period, use a backup birth control method (such as condoms) for the first 7 days.
missed_dose: If you left the ring in for more than 3 weeks but less than 4 weeks (28 days total), remove it and take your 7-day ring-free break as usual — you are still protected. If the ring has been in for more than 4 weeks, remove it and use a backup birth control method until a new ring has been in place for 7 days, and take a pregnancy test. If the ring was out of the vagina for less than 3 hours, rinse it with cool water and reinsert it — you are still protected. If the ring was out for 3 hours or more, reinsert it and use a backup method (like condoms) for the next 7 days. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Unopened rings: Store in a refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Rings can also be stored at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for up to 4 months. Do not store above 77°F (25°C) or expose to direct sunlight. Keep away from children and pets. Do not freeze. After removal, place the used ring in the foil pouch it came in and throw it away in the trash — do not flush it down the toilet.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking while using this ring, especially if you are over 35 years old — it greatly increases the risk of serious heart and blood vessel problems. Do not use other vaginal products (such as spermicides or certain antifungal creams inserted into the vagina) without checking with your doctor first, as some may damage the ring. Avoid using the ring at the same time as a diaphragm, as it may not fit properly. Tell your doctor about all medications you take, including herbal supplements like St. John's Wort, as some medications can make the ring less effective at preventing pregnancy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden severe chest pain or shortness of breath; sudden severe headache; vision changes or loss of vision; severe stomach or abdominal pain; weakness, numbness, or tingling in your arms or legs; calf pain or swelling (possible blood clot); yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); severe depression or mood changes; signs of a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing). Also call your doctor if you miss a period, if the ring keeps slipping out, if you have unusual vaginal discharge or odor, or if you cannot remove the ring.
when_it_works: If you start the ring on the first day of your period, you are protected from pregnancy right away. If you start it on any other day of your cycle, you need to use a backup birth control method (such as condoms) for the first 7 days. The ring is about 91–99% effective at preventing pregnancy when used correctly and consistently.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this ring if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. Breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using this ring while breastfeeding — it may reduce milk supply and small amounts of hormones may pass into breast milk. Teenagers: This ring can be used by teenagers who have started their menstrual periods. Older adults: This ring is not typically used after menopause. Women over 35 who smoke should NOT use this ring due to a significantly increased risk of serious cardiovascular events. Women with a history of blood clots, stroke, heart attack, certain types of migraines, liver disease, or certain cancers should talk to their doctor before using this ring, as it may not be safe for them.
